For over a year, Jesus lived in Zebedee's home, working and fishing with James, John, and David, living the life of a skilled fisherman and boatbuilder [129:1.4]~5.
42.018.h4: 2) Social Activities as a Resident of Capernaum
42.019.p: Jesus registered for taxation as a "skilled craftsman of Capernaum" and was known as a resident of Capernaum until the end of his earth life [129:1.8]. He studied in the library of the Capernaum synagogue, mingled with the young people, listened to their interests, and engaged in deep conversations about politics, sociology, and philosophy at the evening gatherings in Zebedee's home [129:1.10]. The workers of Zebedee learned to love Jesus and began to call him "Master" [129:1.11].
42.020.h4: 3) Financial Settlement and Trust with John
42.021.p: In his twenty-eighth year (A.D. 22), before leaving for Jerusalem, Jesus asked John, the son of Zebedee, to handle the support of his family [129:2.3]. John chose a wise plan, using Jesus' money to buy a house in Capernaum in trust and using the income to assist Jesus' family [129:2.4]. The family in Nazareth, unaware of this arrangement with John, believed Jesus had ceased to help them, leading them to become self-sustaining under James's leadership [129:2.5].
42.022.h3: 4. The Mediterranean Tour and Completion of Human Experience
42.023.h4: 1) Accepting Tutorship for an Indian Traveler
42.024.p: In Jerusalem, Jesus met a wealthy traveler from India who was looking for an interpreter and a tutor for his son, and Jesus accepted the position on the condition of receiving a year's wages in advance for his family [129:2.9]. Jesus turned this large sum over to John to care for the family and informed no one of his whereabouts except Zebedee, not even his family or the apostles [129:2.10].
42.025.h4: 2) Tour of the Mediterranean and Experience of Humanity
42.026.p: In his twenty-ninth year (A.D. 23), Jesus toured the Roman world, known as the Scribe of Damascus or a Jewish tutor [129:3.2]. The real purpose of this tour was to know mankind, and he met and loved hundreds of diverse people—rich and poor, educated and uneducated, moral and immoral [129:3.8]. Through this experience, he completed his training in educational contact with the peoples of the Mediterranean basin and learned virtually all there was to know of how men lived and existed [129:3.7].
42.027.h4: 3) Divine-Human Integration and Preparation for Ministry
42.028.p: During this tour, Jesus made great progress in his relationship with the indwelling Adjuster and came to know with human certainty that he was a Creator Son of the Universal Father [129:3.9]. Having experienced human emotions, joys and sorrows, and all phases of life, Jesus lived the full life of a mortal and received the unqualified acceptance of the Universal Father [129:4.6]. By the end of his twenty-ninth year, Jesus had virtually finished the life required of mortals and reached the perfection of humanity, awaiting the time to appear before God [129:4.8].
43.title: Jesus’ Trip to Rome
43.001.h3: 1. The Journey to Rome and Lessons of the Mediterranean
43.002.h4: 1) The Story of Jonah and the Nature of Good and Evil
43.003.p: While Jesus and his party stayed at Joppa, Jesus became friends with a truth-seeking Philistine youth named Gadiah; Jesus taught him to look beyond the traditional interpretation of the Jonah story, explaining that we are all Jonahs who often seek to flee from present duty and the will of God, and that such flight from duty is the sacrifice of truth [130:1.2]. Jesus also clarified that God did not create evil, explaining that evil is the result of the immature choices and mistakes of those who resist goodness and are disloyal to truth, likening it to the inevitable darkness that follows the unwise rejection of light [130:1.5]. Although God has endowed man with the power of choice, thereby creating the potential for evil, such errors do not actually exist until an intelligent creature willfully mischooses, and these are later transformed into sin through deliberate rebellion [130:1.6].
43.004.h4: 2) Human Ministry in Caesarea and the Soul of Animals
43.005.p: At Caesarea, while helping at a boatyard, Jesus taught the worker Anaxand that even a wicked foreman could be a means to make him a better man, like salt, reminding him of the value of being a channel of light to those in spiritual darkness [130:2.4]. When Ganid asked Jesus why he constantly took an interest in strangers, Jesus replied that to one who knows God, there are no strangers, and one discovers that all men are brethren [130:2.6]. Furthermore, when Ganid asked about the soul of a dog, Jesus explained that while animals possess a mind, they lack a spiritual nature and cannot experience spiritual emotions; what makes a human a moral being is the possession of spiritual discrimination and the power of truth choice [130:2.8].
43.006.h4: 3) The Lighthouse of Alexandria and the Discourse on Reality
43.007.p: Upon arriving in Alexandria and viewing the Pharos lighthouse, Jesus told Ganid that when he returned to India, he should be like that lighthouse to those in darkness, becoming a light of life and guiding them to the harbor of salvation [130:3.2]. After interpreting for a professor of Platonic philosophy, Jesus explained to Ganid that the source of universe reality is the Infinite and that the finite creation is the time-space repercussion of the eternal mind of God [130:4.1], [130:4.2]. Jesus taught that neither the scientist nor the mystic should view the world with one eye, and that the depth of universe reality is revealed when the facts perceived by the material mind are harmonized with the true values discerned by the spiritualized intellect [130:4.10].
43.008.h4: 4) Mountain Experience in Crete and Overcoming Fear
43.009.p: On the island of Crete, Jesus rescued a slave girl from a drunken brute, displaying a rare use of physical force to protect the weak, yet he forbade Ganid from striking the man in return [130:5.4]. To a fearful youth named Fortune whom they met in the mountains, Jesus encouraged him to refuse to be a slave to fear, urging him to let the spirit within stimulate his mind to conquer fear through the power of faith and return to his duty, eventually transforming him into a leader of the Cretan Christians [130:6.5].
43.010.h3: 2. Sojourn in Rome and Preparation for the Future
43.011.p: 1) Interaction with Religious Leaders and Preparation for Mission: Jesus stayed in Rome for six months and associated intimately with 32 religious leaders of the time (Cynics, Stoics, mystery cults, etc.); he never attacked their errors but selected the truths they held, embellishing and illuminating them [132:0.4]. This ministry of Jesus laid the foundation for the rapid spread of Christianity when Peter and Paul later arrived in Rome, and 30 of those taught by Jesus became pivotal individuals in establishing Roman Christianity [132:0.5]. Jesus taught them personally, and they never realized that the scribe they conversed with was Jesus, the very subject of the religion they would later embrace [132:0.9].
43.012.h4: 2) True Values and the Standard of Good and Evi
43.013.p: Jesus warned Angamon, a Stoic leader, that the standard of true values must be found in the spiritual world and eternal reality, and that the development of a purely material science without moral insight could become a threat to civilization [132:1.2], [132:1.3]. To the Cynic leader Mardus, he taught that good and evil are relative, and that goodness is always living, exists in personal experience, and is correlated with the discernment of truth and beauty [132:2.7]. Jesus explained that the shadow of potential evil does not fully disappear until man reaches the Paradise levels and is exposed to the perfect light, but as the desire for goodness grows, evil diminishes [132:2.6], [132:2.9].
43.014.h4: 3) Counsel to the Wealthy Regarding Material Possessions
43.015.p: Jesus advised a wealthy Roman citizen to administer his wealth as a trust for the benefit of society and future generations, analyzing the ten sources of wealth—inherited, discovered, trade, unfair, interest, genius, accidental, stolen, trust funds, and earned—to explain their differing moral responsibilities [132:5.2]. Jesus particularly emphasized that wealth derived from exploiting labor or enslavement brings a spiritual stigma, and that unjustly acquired wealth must be restored to its owners to cleanse one's possessions. This rich man was deeply moved by Jesus' counsel and pledged to administer his fortune with justice and mercy [132:5.25].
43.016.h4: 4) The Indifferent Pagan and the Appraisal of Buddha
43.017.p: While touring the environs of Rome, Jesus explained to Ganid that one cannot force the teaching of God upon an indifferent pagan who does not hunger for truth, and that God cannot be revealed to one who does not seek Him [132:7.2]. When Gonod asked about the Buddha in the Swiss mountains, Jesus evaluated Buddha as a great prophet who was a "spiritual orphan" because he lost sight of the Father in heaven, resulting in the tragedy of teaching a philosophy without God [132:7.4]. Jesus pointed out that Buddhism is like a ship stranded just outside the harbor, and unless they grasp the noble spirit of Buddha, it will be difficult for them to enter the haven of spiritual rest [132:7.4].
43.018.h3: 3. Events and Teachings on the Return from Rome
43.020.p: On the way to Tarentum, Jesus rescued a small boy by restraining a rough youth (mercy), but when Ganid wanted to strike the attacker, Jesus stopped him, teaching that the administration of justice is the function of the social or universe administrative groups, not personal vengeance [133:1.1]~2. When Ganid asked about self-defense, Jesus stated that while he would defend himself against an attacker lacking moral judgment, he would not attack a fellow human being or seek private revenge, placing absolute trust in the protection of the Father in heaven [133:1.4].
43.021.h4: 2) Equality in the Home and Respect for Women
43.022.p: Witnessing a husband mistreating his wife at the landing, Jesus approached him and taught that no man has the right to rule over a woman unless she voluntarily grants him that authority, and that men and women are equal partners who cooperate with God in creating children [133:2.2]. Jesus emphasized that if a man loves his children as God does, he must cherish his wife, who is a spiritual partner, a teaching that led Gonod to resolve to reorganize his family life upon returning to India, [133:2.3].
43.023.h4: 3) The Prostitutes of Corinth and Spiritual Vision
43.024.p: In Corinth, when Ganid spoke roughly to prostitutes and tried to dismiss them, Jesus pointed out that they were not willfully evil but had chosen that path due to cruel fate and poverty, stating that we do not have the right to judge them [133:3.6]~7. Jesus saw sorrow rather than evil in their tear-stained faces, took them to the home of his friend Justus, shared a meal with them, and helped them to live a new life by reminding them that they were beloved children of God [133:3.8]~9.
43.025.h4: 4) Science and the Unity of Religion in Athens
43.026.p: In Athens, Jesus debated with a Greek scientist, teaching that while science deals with energy and facts and religion deals with values, true philosophy must unite the two through wisdom [133:5.4]. Jesus warned that a purely physical scientist may fall into spiritual blindness through mathematical pride, explaining that the true unity of the universe is found when one recognizes that both quantitative facts and qualitative values have a common cause in the Paradise Father [133:5.8].
43.027.h4: 5) Soul and Mind in Ephesus and Cyprus
43.028.p: In Ephesus, Jesus defined the soul as being born of the union of the moral self of man and the indwelling divine spirit, which elevates man above the animal level and gives him eternal survival value [133:6.5]. In Cyprus, he taught Ganid that human self-consciousness is not merely the sum of sensations but is achieved through integration with the indwelling spirit, and that physical senses alone can never attain spiritual levels [133:7.9]~10. At the end of the journey in Ur of Mesopotamia, Jesus discussed the differences between knowledge, wisdom, and truth and bid farewell to his Indian friends; Ganid later heard of the crucified Jesus and recognized the similarity to the teachings of his former tutor Joshua, but never knew they were the same person, [133:9.5].
